idiom_name: Array.prototype.map (+ Promise.prototype.then for the async context)
implementation_notes: Array.prototype.map is the language's built-in instance: it calls the callback once per element and returns a new array of the same length, replacing the index loop and its accumulator - MDN documents it as creating a new array 'populated with the results of calling a provided function on every element', skipping holes in sparse arrays and passing (element, index, array) to the callback. Promises carry the same operation under another name, Promise.prototype.then, so an async pipeline maps without leaving its context, and optional chaining (?.) covers only the single absent-value case rather than a reusable context. The classic form is always the method here; the only real choice is whether the context is an array (eager) or an iterator (lazy).
pitfalls: Callbacks receive (element, index, array): ['1','2'].map(parseInt) yields [1, NaN] because parseInt takes the index as its radix - wrap the function in a lambda.
map skips holes in sparse arrays but keeps them in the result, and it allocates a full new array per stage even when a later stage discards most elements.
There is no built-in optional context: mapping a possibly-undefined value is optional chaining plus a default, and a missing receiver throws (TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined).

variants.name: Iterator helper methods (lazy, over any iterable)
variants.implementation_notes: The iterator protocol carries the same operation lazily: Iterator.prototype.map returns an iterator helper that applies the mapping function when the next value is requested, and Iterator.from wraps any iterable or array-like into an iterator that has the helpers. MDN states the difference from the array form directly - iterator helpers 'are lazy, meaning that they only produce the next value when requested' - so a chain over a generator, a Map/Set iterator or a paged source materialises nothing and an upstream take(n) stops the work. It replaces the hand-written generator pipeline (function* stages composed with yield) and is the right context when the source is unbounded or expensive; the array form stays the default for in-memory data.
pitfalls: Nothing runs without a consuming method (toArray, reduce, for...of), and an unterminated chain over an infinite source never ends.
Availability is runtime-dependent: the helpers are Baseline since 2025, older Node and browser versions need a polyfill, and plain JavaScript gives no compile-time warning.
The helper consumes the underlying iterator: the source cannot be re-iterated, unlike an array.
